defaults: Opening states a viewer problem or analytical question, not an API description or generic pattern summary
Has at least one 'when not to use' or 'when to avoid' section with concrete reasons
No sections that are pure reorganized API docs without rationale for when/why to use them
Rules and recommendations include failure modes, perceptual reasons, or concrete consequences
Related skills are cross-referenced where the reader would need them
Code examples demonstrate non-obvious design choices, not boilerplate setup
Pitfalls explain what goes wrong and why, not just what to avoid

annotation: Has editorial judgment guidance: what deserves a callout, hierarchy of emphasis
responsive: Covers D3-specific responsive decisions (tick density at narrow widths, margin scaling), not just ResizeObserver mechanics
small-multiples: Addresses when to share vs. separate scales, with consequences of each choice
sparkcharts: Covers when sparkcharts mislead (baseline, truncation, aspect ratio)
data-table: Frames tables as a first-class representation, not a fallback
navigation: Addresses when NOT to add zoom (most charts shouldn't)
network: Addresses when network visualization is the wrong choice entirely
visual-texture: Covers perceptual ordering of textures (which patterns read as more vs less)
hierarchy-layouts: Has layout selection guidance mapping each layout to the viewer question it answers
hierarchy-interaction: Addresses when expand/collapse hurts (hides context needed for comparison)
linked-views: Addresses coordination pitfalls (feedback loops, update storms, cognitive overload)
distributions: Box plot bimodality trap is called out explicitly
KDE bandwidth framed as an editorial judgment, not a technical parameter
time-series: Horizon chart usage has perceptual research backing (band count guidance)
scales: Log vs symlog decision is covered with concrete failure mode (zeros)
force: Addresses when force layout is the wrong choice
shape-morphing: Addresses when morphing misleads (false continuity between categorically different states)
data-gathering: Has data smells section connecting bad data to specific visual bugs
edge-bundling: Beta parameter framed as a judgment call with false-connection tradeoff
webgl: Honestly addresses when you don't need WebGL (Canvas handles 100K+ fine)
square-tool: Each convention explains what breaks when violated AND when breaking it is correct
jig-tool: Each archetype describes the viewer experience it produces, not just code structure
